chapters.t: In the very beginning, God made the sky and the earth. There was nothing else at all — only God.
Everything was dark and empty, and God’s Spirit moved over the deep water like a soft wind.
Then God said, “Let there be light!” And light came. God saw that the light was good.
God called the light “day” and the dark “night”. That was the very first day.
On the second day God made the wide sky above and the deep sea below.
On the third day God gathered the water together so that dry land could appear.
God covered the land with grass and flowers and tall trees full of fruit. It was good.
On the fourth day God set the sun in the sky for the day, and the moon and stars for the night.
On the fifth day God filled the sea with fish and the sky with birds, and told them to spread everywhere.
On the sixth day God made every animal that walks — big ones, small ones, and every one in between.
Then God made people, a man and a woman, in his own likeness, to care for the world he had made.
God blessed them and gave the whole good earth into their hands.
God looked at everything he had made, and it was very good indeed.
On the seventh day God had finished his work, so he rested.
God blessed the seventh day and made it special, a day to stop and be glad.
God planted a beautiful garden in a place called Eden, and put the man there.
A river ran through the garden, and every kind of good tree grew beside it.
God said, “You may eat from any tree here. Only one tree you must leave alone.”
God brought the animals to the man, and whatever he called each one, that became its name.
God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone.” So God made a woman to stand beside him.
The man and the woman were friends together in the garden, and they were not ashamed.
A crafty snake came to the woman and asked, “Did God really say you must not eat from that tree?”
“God only said it to keep something from you,” said the snake. That was not true.
The fruit looked lovely. The woman took some and ate it, and the man ate some too.
At once they felt afraid, and they hid among the trees.
God called, “Where are you?” — not because he did not know, but because he wanted them to answer.
The man blamed the woman, and the woman blamed the snake. Nobody wanted to say sorry.
Because they had not listened, they had to leave the beautiful garden.
But God made warm clothes for them, and promised that one day he would put everything right.
The man and woman had two sons. Cain grew crops, and Abel looked after sheep.
Both brothers brought a gift to God. Abel brought his very best.
Cain grew angry and his face fell.
God said kindly, “Why are you angry? If you do what is right, you can lift your head up.”
But Cain would not listen, and he hurt his brother Abel.
God was very sad. Even so, he still watched over Cain and kept him safe.
Years went by, and the family of the first people grew and grew.
Fathers had sons, and those sons had sons, and their names were remembered.
One of them was called Enoch. Enoch walked with God as a friend walks with a friend.
Another was Methuselah, who lived longer than anyone in the story.
And in that long line a man was born named Noah.
As the world filled with people, it also filled with unkindness, and God was grieved.
But Noah listened to God, and God was pleased with him.
God told Noah, “Build a great boat of wood — an ark — with rooms inside and a door in the side.”
“Bring your family inside, and two of every kind of animal, so that they may live.”
It was a very big job, and it took a very long time. Noah did everything God asked.
When the ark was ready, the animals came in two by two, and Noah’s family went in too.
Then God shut the door behind them.
The rain began, and it fell for forty days and forty nights.
The water rose higher and higher, until even the hills were covered.
But the ark floated safely on top of the water, and everyone inside was kept safe.
God did not forget Noah, not for one moment.
God sent a wind, and slowly, slowly the water began to go down.
The ark came to rest on a mountain, and the tops of the hills peeped out.
Noah sent out a raven, and then a dove, to see if the ground was dry.
The dove found nowhere to land and came back, so Noah waited seven more days.
This time the dove came back with a fresh olive leaf in her beak. Land at last!
Then everyone came out of the ark onto the good dry ground, and Noah thanked God.
God blessed Noah and his family and said, “Fill the earth again.”
God made a promise: “Never again will a flood cover the whole earth.”
“I am putting my rainbow in the clouds,” said God. “It is the sign of my promise.”
So whenever the rain stops and the colours arch across the sky, they remember.
God keeps his promises — always.
Noah’s sons had children, and those children had children of their own.
The families spread out across the whole world.
Some went to the hills, some to the coasts, some to the wide open plains.
Each family had its own land and its own way of speaking.
At first everyone in the world spoke the very same language.
They found a wide flat place and said, “Let us build a city, and a tower that reaches the sky.”
“Then everyone will look at us,” they said, “and we will make a great name for ourselves.”
God came down to see the tower they were so proud of.
He gave them different languages, so that they could no longer understand one another.
So they stopped building, and went to live all over the earth, just as God had said.
